summary: A best current practice recommending that bidirectional RTP and RTCP sessions use one UDP port pair for both directions, commonly called symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP. Doing so makes such sessions easier to handle through NATs and firewalls.

eli5.summary: Instead of using one door to talk and another to listen, use the same door both ways so it is easier to find and let through.

questions: rtp and rtcp port usage best practice
why does nat need symmetric rtp
subtitle: Send and receive RTP and RTCP from the same UDP port, which NATs and firewalls expect.

tldr.problem: RTP and RTCP run over UDP, which does not require the same port for sending and receiving. Many firewalls, NATs and RTP implementations expect the same port in both directions and do not work with asymmetric RTP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines symmetric RTP and symmetric RTCP: a device receiving on a given UDP port and IP address also transmits from that same port and address. It recommends that this always be used for bidirectional streams.
tldr.outcome: Symmetric ports are REQUIRED behind NATs without an integrated ALG and with media relays, and helpful elsewhere. The one drawback noted is that an attacker who sees one packet can attack either endpoint.

facts.label: Required for
facts.value: NATs without ALG, and media relays

today: RFC 4961 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 131, July 2007), and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Symmetry Needs a Definition
sections.content:
TCP is inherently bidirectional and uses the same local port to send and receive. UDP is not, and does not require it. Some UDP applications use one port for both directions (the RFC gives DNS as an example), some use different ports with explicit signaling (TFTP), and some, like RTP, do not specify the choice.

Because of this, using one port for both directions has generally been ignored for RTP and RTCP. Yet many firewalls, Network Address Translators (NATs) and RTP implementations expect symmetric RTP and do not work with asymmetric RTP. The term had never been defined, and this RFC defines it.

Each device picks the port it receives on and the port it transmits from. For unicast flows the receive port is communicated to the peer, for example in SDP carried in SIP. There is no correspondence between the local and remote ports: device A may use 1234 but device B cannot be forced to, since it may already use that port for something else.
sections.eli5: Mail carriers get confused if you send letters from one house and wait for replies at another. This note says to use one house for both.

sections.title: What Symmetric RTP and RTCP Mean
sections.content:
A device supports symmetric RTP if, when it receives a bidirectional RTP stream on UDP port A and IP address a, it also transmits RTP for that stream from the same source port A and address a. In short, it uses the same UDP port to transmit and receive one RTP stream.

A device that does not do this transmits RTP from a different port or a different IP address than the one it receives on.

Symmetric RTCP is defined the same way for the control stream: receiving RTCP on port B and address b means transmitting RTCP from that same port B and address b. RTP and RTCP are treated separately, each with its own port.
sections.eli5: If you listen at door number A, you also knock from door number A. The same goes for the separate control channel, which has its own door.

sections.title: When to Use It
sections.content:
Symmetric RTP and RTCP are REQUIRED in two specific cases.

  • NATs without an integrated Application Layer Gateway (ALG). Such NATs need endpoints to use symmetric UDP ports to establish bidirectional traffic. This holds for all NAT types described in RFC 4787.
  • Session Border Controllers and other relays such as TURN. Relays are needed to cross a NAT that is Address-Dependent or Address and Port-Dependent, but even with a relay, symmetric ports are still required to traverse such a NAT.
sections.eli5: Some gatekeepers will only let your reply through if it comes back through the same door you used. Using one door also makes it easier to find problems.

sections.title: Benefits Beyond the Required Cases
sections.content:
Symmetric RTP and RTCP are also helpful, though not required, in other situations. A firewall that can expect symmetric RTP and RTCP can keep its dynamic per-call port filter list more restrictive than it could for asymmetric RTP and RTCP. Debugging and troubleshooting are also easier.

Other UDP-based protocols can benefit from common local transmit and receive ports too. The RFC knows of no cases where symmetric RTP or symmetric RTCP are harmful, so it RECOMMENDS that they always be used for bidirectional RTP media streams.
sections.eli5: Even when nobody forces you, one door is easier for guards to watch and easier to fix when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If an attacker learns the source and destination UDP ports of a symmetric RTP or RTCP flow, the attacker can send RTP or RTCP packets to that host. With asymmetric flows, the attacker would first have to learn the ports used for the reverse traffic.

So with symmetric ports an attacker need only see one RTP or RTCP packet to attack either endpoint. The RFC notes this is similar to other UDP protocols that use one port pair, such as DNS.
sections.eli5: If you use the same door both ways, someone who spots that door once knows how to reach you.
